passages.title: Creation
passages.summary: In the beginning God creates the heavens and the earth. He speaks, and light, sky, land, and plants appear over three days. Sun, moon, stars, sea animals, and birds follow. On the sixth day he makes land animals and then people. He makes people in his own image, male and female. He blesses them and tells them to fill the earth and rule the animals. He gives plants as food to people and animals. God sees all he has made and calls it very good.
passages.uncertainty: The map has no sure location for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 2 places human creation within God’s work. Verse 27 says God made male and female in his image. How should that shape the way you treat people?

contextNote.title: Creation gives people a shared worth
contextNote.text: Six times the chapter says God saw that his work was good. People come last, and verse 31 says “very good.” Verse 27 says “image” twice and then names both male and female. No one group holds that standing alone. The command to rule in verse 28 comes after the blessing. Verses 29–30 then give plants as food to people and animals alike. So ruling here sits beside care for life that God called good.

passages.title: Life in the garden
passages.summary: God finishes his work, rests on the seventh day, and makes that day holy. Then the LORD God forms a man from dust and breathes life into him. God plants a garden in Eden with a river and two named trees. He puts the man there to work it and keep it. He forbids one tree and warns of death. God says it is not good for the man to be alone. The man names the animals, but none is a helper like him. God makes a woman from his rib, and the man welcomes her as his flesh.
passages.uncertainty: The map has no sure location for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 3 connects the garden with God’s commands. The man has work and food but is alone (verse 18). What need does the woman answer in verse 23?

contextNote.title: Work does not answer every human need
contextNote.text: Chapter 1 said “good” again and again. Verse 18 is the first “not good.” The man already has a garden, food, and work (verses 15–16). In verses 19–20 he meets every animal and names it. Naming shows he knows them, yet none is “comparable to him.” Only then does God make the woman. The man’s words in verse 23 are about likeness: bone of his bones.

passages.title: The Fall
passages.summary: The serpent asks the woman what God really said. She repeats the command, and the serpent says she will not die. She sees the fruit is good, eats, and gives some to her husband. Their eyes open, and they cover themselves and hide. God asks where the man is and whether he ate. The man blames the woman, and the woman blames the serpent. God curses the serpent and the ground, and speaks of pain and hard work. He clothes them with skins and sends them out of Eden.
passages.uncertainty: The map has no sure location for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 4 expands the garden account. Second Nephi 2 connects the Fall with choice and redemption. The man answers God by blaming two others (verse 12). Whom does he blame?

contextNote.title: Blame changes the relationships in the garden
contextNote.text: God asks the man two direct questions in verses 9 and 11. Verse 12 answers neither one first. The man names the woman, and then names God as the one who gave her. “I ate” comes last. In 2:23 he called her bone of his bones. Now he puts her between himself and God. Verse 13 shows the same move when the woman points to the serpent.

passages.title: Cain and Abel
passages.summary: Eve bears Cain and then Abel. Cain farms, and Abel keeps sheep. Both bring offerings, and the LORD accepts Abel’s but not Cain’s. The LORD warns Cain that sin crouches at the door. Cain kills Abel in the field and asks if he is his brother’s keeper. The LORD sends Cain away as a wanderer but marks him for protection. Cain’s family builds a city, and Lamech boasts of killing a man. Eve bears Seth, and people begin to call on the LORD’s name.
passages.uncertainty: The map has no sure location for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 5 adds gospel teaching after the Fall. The LORD warns Cain before he kills (verse 7). What does the warning say Cain can still do?

contextNote.title: Protection becomes a claim to unlimited revenge
contextNote.text: Verse 15 sets a limit. God promises sevenfold vengeance to stop anyone from killing Cain. In verse 24 Lamech takes that promise for himself and multiplies it. He has killed a young man for a wound (verse 23). No one gave him this protection. A rule meant to hold back killing becomes a boast about killing. Verse 26 ends with a different use of speech: calling on the LORD’s name.

passages.title: Generations to Noah
passages.summary: This is the family record from Adam to Noah. God made people in his likeness, and Adam fathers Seth in his own likeness. Each entry gives a father’s age, his son, his total years, and his death. The years are very long, up to 969 for Methuselah. Enoch’s entry is different. He walks with God, and God takes him. Lamech names his son Noah and hopes for comfort from the cursed ground. Noah fathers Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
passages.uncertainty: The map has no sure location for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 6–7 expands Enoch’s account. Every entry but one ends with “then he died.” What does verse 24 say about Enoch?

contextNote.title: One life breaks the repeated ending
contextNote.text: The chapter repeats one pattern eight times and ends each with “then he died.” Genesis 2:17 warned of death, and the list shows it arriving. Enoch breaks the pattern in verses 22–24. The text says twice that he “walked with God.” His entry has no death line. It says God took him. Verse 29 adds a second break: a father hopes his son will bring relief.

passages.title: Noah builds the ark
passages.summary: People multiply, and God’s sons take human daughters as wives. The LORD says man’s days will be 120 years. He sees that human thoughts are evil all the time, and he is grieved. He decides to wipe out people and animals. But Noah finds favor and walks with God. God tells Noah the earth is filled with violence. He orders a ship of gopher wood with three levels and one door. Noah is to bring his family, pairs of animals, and food, and he obeys.
passages.uncertainty: The map has no sure location for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 8 describes Noah’s preaching before the flood. Verse 9 says Noah “walked with God.” What does verse 22 say he did with God’s orders?

contextNote.title: The flood account begins with violence
contextNote.text: Verse 5 gives the cause of the flood as seen in the human heart. Verse 11 gives it as seen on the ground: violence fills the earth. The word “corrupt” appears three times in verses 11–12. God’s word for what he will do in verse 13 is “destroy.” The earth is already ruined by its people before the water comes. Verse 6 shows the decision costs God grief. Verse 8 keeps one door open: Noah finds favor.

passages.title: The flood
passages.summary: The LORD tells Noah to enter the ship with his household. Noah takes seven pairs of clean animals and one pair of the others. Noah is six hundred years old. After seven days the deep bursts open and the sky’s windows open. Rain falls forty days and nights. Noah’s family and the animals go in, and the LORD shuts him in. The water lifts the ship and covers the high mountains. Everything on dry land dies, and only those in the ship remain.
passages.uncertainty: The map has no sure location for this chapter.

lds.text: The Church manual reads Noah’s deliverance within God’s dealings with humanity. Verse 5 says Noah did all the LORD commanded. What does the LORD do for Noah in verse 16?

contextNote.title: The closed door marks the limit of safety
contextNote.text: Noah builds the ship and loads it, as verses 5 and 9 say. One act is not his: closing the door. Verse 16 says “the LORD shut him in.” Noah’s safety rests on that act, not on his building alone. The closed door keeps the family in and the water out. It also marks the end of the time to enter. Verse 23 states the result: only those inside are left.

passages.title: The waters recede
passages.summary: God remembers Noah and the animals and sends a wind. The water goes down, and the ship rests on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sends out a raven and then a dove. The dove comes back with an olive leaf, then does not return. God tells Noah to leave the ship with his family and the animals. Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings. The LORD says he will not again curse the ground or strike every living thing. Seedtime and harvest, summer and winter, day and night will not stop.

lds.text: Noah worships after deliverance. Verse 1 says God “remembered Noah.” What does God promise about seasons in verse 22?

contextNote.title: The promise concerns ordinary seasons
contextNote.text: Verse 21 gives a surprising reason for the promise. The human heart is still “evil from his youth,” as in 6:5. The flood did not change people. What changes is what God says he will do. Verse 22 puts the promise in farm terms: planting, harvest, cold, heat. People can plan a year because these will come. Noah’s first act on dry ground is an offering, not a field (verse 20).

passages.title: A covenant with Noah
passages.summary: God blesses Noah and his sons and tells them to fill the earth. Animals will fear them, and they may eat meat but not blood. God will demand a reckoning for human life, because he made people in his image. He makes a covenant with Noah, his family, and every living creature. No flood will destroy the earth again, and the rainbow is the sign. Noah plants a vineyard and gets drunk. Ham sees his father naked, and Shem and Japheth cover him. Noah curses Canaan and blesses Shem and Japheth.
passages.uncertainty: The map has no sure location for this chapter.

lds.text: A covenant is a sacred agreement. Verse 6 gives a reason not to shed human blood. What is the reason?

contextNote.title: Shared worth sets a limit on killing
contextNote.text: After the flood, people may kill animals for food (verse 3). Verse 5 draws a line at human life. Verse 6 gives the reason: “God made man in his own image.” That is the same ground given for human worth in 1:27. The flood did not remove it. So the rule protects every person, not one family or rank. The earth was “filled with violence” in 6:11, and this rule answers that.

passages.title: Families and nations
passages.summary: This is the family record of Noah’s sons after the flood. Japheth’s line spreads to the coasts and islands. Ham’s line includes Cush, Mizraim, and Canaan. Cush’s son Nimrod is a mighty hunter, and his kingdom begins at Babel. Canaan’s families spread from Sidon toward Gaza. Shem’s line includes Eber, Peleg, and Joktan. Each list ends with families, languages, lands, and nations. From these families the nations spread over the earth.

lds.text: The family record joins many peoples to common ancestors. Verse 32 says the nations came from one family. How should that shape the way one nation sees another?

contextNote.title: Family language places nations within one world
contextNote.text: The chapter lists many peoples as one family tree. Peoples who later fight Israel appear in it as relatives. Canaan, Assyria, and the Philistines all have a place (verses 11, 14, 15). The refrain in verses 5, 20, and 31 names families, languages, lands, and nations. So difference in language is treated as normal here. Verse 32 sums it up: all nations come from Noah’s sons. Chapter 11 then tells how the languages divided.

passages.title: Babel and Terah's family
passages.summary: All people speak one language and settle on a plain in Shinar. They bake bricks and plan a city with a tower to the sky. They want a name for themselves and fear being scattered. The LORD comes down to see, confuses their language, and scatters them. The city is called Babel. Then the record runs from Shem to Terah. Terah fathers Abram, Nahor, and Haran, and Abram’s wife Sarai has no child. Terah leaves Ur for Canaan but settles in Haran and dies there.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: The Church manual contrasts Babel with the covenant family story. The builders want “a name for ourselves” (verse 4). Who promises a great name in 12:2?

contextNote.title: A great name competes with spreading across the earth
contextNote.text: Verse 4 gives the builders two aims. They want a name, and they want not to be scattered. God had told people to fill the earth in 1:28 and 9:1. The tower should reach the sky, yet the LORD “came down” to see it. They get the very thing they feared: scattering (verse 8). In 12:2 God offers Abram a great name as a gift. The chapter sets a name people grab beside a name God gives.

passages.title: Abram's call
passages.summary: The LORD tells Abram to leave his country and his father’s house. He promises a great nation and a blessing for all families through Abram. Abram goes at age seventy-five with Sarai and Lot. In Canaan the LORD promises the land to his offspring, and Abram builds altars. A famine sends him to Egypt. He asks Sarai to say she is his sister, because he fears being killed. Pharaoh takes her and pays Abram well, and the LORD sends plagues. Pharaoh rebukes Abram and sends them away.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Abraham 2 links the covenant with blessing all families. Verse 3 promises blessing to “all the families of the earth.” What happens to Pharaoh’s house when Abram hides the truth (verse 17)?

contextNote.title: A promise reaches beyond the chosen household
contextNote.text: The promise in verses 2–3 has seven parts and ends outside Abram’s family. All the families of the earth are to be blessed through him. The rest of the chapter tests that at once. In Egypt Abram protects himself with a false story (verse 13). Pharaoh’s house gets plagues, not blessing (verse 17). A foreign king then corrects the man God chose (verses 18–19). The promise stands, but the chapter shows it does not depend on Abram’s good conduct.

passages.title: Abram and Lot separate
passages.summary: Abram returns from Egypt to Bethel, rich in livestock, silver, and gold. Lot also has flocks, and the land cannot hold both. Their herdsmen quarrel. Abram asks for no strife and offers Lot his choice of land. Lot sees the well-watered Jordan plain and chooses it. He camps near Sodom, whose men are very wicked. The LORD tells Abram to look all around, for the land will be his. Abram moves to the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and builds an altar.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Abraham gives Lot the first choice. What reason does Abram give for ending the quarrel in verse 8?

contextNote.title: Giving the first choice limits a family conflict
contextNote.text: Abram is the uncle, and the land was promised to him (12:7). He could choose first. Verse 9 gives the choice to Lot. His stated reason in verse 8 is “we are relatives.” Verse 10 shows Lot choosing by what his eyes see. Verse 13 warns what was near that green plain. After Lot leaves, the LORD tells Abram to look, and gives him all.

passages.title: Lot rescued
passages.summary: Four kings make war on five kings near the Salt Sea. The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah flee, and the winners take goods, food, and people. They take Lot, who lives in Sodom. Abram leads 318 trained men, attacks by night, and brings everyone back. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine. He blesses Abram, and Abram gives him a tenth. The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods. Abram refuses even a thread, so the king cannot say he made Abram rich.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Alma 13 expands Melchizedek’s role as a priest. Keep that teaching distinct from Genesis’s brief account. Abram gives to one king and refuses another (verses 20–23). What reason does he give?

contextNote.title: Rescue need not create dependence on a ruler
contextNote.text: Two kings meet Abram after the battle. Melchizedek blesses him and credits God with the win (verse 20). Abram gives him a tenth. The king of Sodom offers goods, and Abram takes nothing. Verse 23 gives his reason: no king may say, “I have made Abram rich.” A gift from a ruler could become a claim on him. Verse 24 keeps his rule from costing his allies their share.

passages.title: God's covenant with Abram
passages.summary: The LORD comes to Abram in a vision and says not to fear. Abram says he has no child, and a servant will be his heir. The LORD says his own son will be his heir and shows him the stars. Abram believes, and the LORD counts it as righteousness. Abram asks how he will know the land is his. He cuts animals in half, and a deep sleep and darkness fall on him. The LORD says his offspring will serve in a foreign land four hundred years. A furnace and a torch pass between the pieces, and the LORD makes a covenant.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: God’s promise meets Abraham’s fear about an heir. Abram asks how he will know (verse 8). What hard news comes with the answer in verse 13?

contextNote.title: The land promise includes a delay marked by suffering
contextNote.text: Abram asks for certainty about the land in verse 8. The answer begins with what he must “know for sure.” His family will be foreigners and slaves for four hundred years. Only then will they come out and return. Verse 16 gives a reason for the wait: the Amorites’ wrong “is not yet full.” So God will not remove a people before its time. In verse 17 only the fire passes between the pieces, while Abram sleeps.

passages.title: Hagar and Ishmael
passages.summary: Sarai has no children and gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram as a wife. Hagar conceives and looks down on Sarai. Sarai blames Abram, and he says Hagar is in her hand. Sarai treats her harshly, and Hagar runs away. The LORD’s angel finds her by a spring and tells her to return. He promises her many offspring and a son named Ishmael, because the LORD heard. Hagar names the LORD “a God who sees.” She bears Ishmael when Abram is eighty-six.

lds.text: God sees Hagar in distress. The angel sends her back but also makes a promise (verses 9–11). What does the name Ishmael say the LORD has done?

contextNote.title: Seeing Hagar does not erase her unequal position
contextNote.text: Hagar has no say in verses 2–3. Sarai gives her, and Abram takes her. The angel is the first to speak to her by name (verse 8). Verse 9 sends her back under Sarai’s hand, and the text does not soften that. Verses 10–11 then give her a promise like Abram’s: offspring too many to count. Her son’s name is tied to the LORD hearing her suffering. In verse 13 she is the one who gives God a name.

passages.title: New names and covenant
passages.summary: Abram is ninety-nine when the LORD appears as God Almighty. God makes a covenant: many nations will come from Abram, and Canaan will be theirs. God changes his name to Abraham. Every male in his house, even bought servants, must be circumcised as the sign. Sarai’s name becomes Sarah, and she will bear a son. Abraham laughs and asks that Ishmael might live before God. God says Sarah will bear Isaac, and Ishmael will also become a great nation. Abraham circumcises every male in his house that same day.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Abraham 2 links covenant blessings with the gospel. Abraham obeys “in the same day” (verse 23). Who in his house receives the sign?

contextNote.title: The covenant sign includes people without equal household power
contextNote.text: God speaks for most of the chapter, and Abraham’s part comes at the end. Verse 23 says he acted “in the same day.” The list of who was circumcised is wide. It names Ishmael, those born in the house, and those bought with money. Verse 21 says the covenant line runs through Isaac, not Ishmael. Yet Ishmael receives the sign and his own blessing (verse 20). The sign covers the whole household, not only the heir.

passages.title: Visitors and Abraham's plea
passages.summary: The LORD appears to Abraham at Mamre as three men stand near his tent. Abraham runs to meet them and serves bread, a calf, butter, and milk. One says Sarah will have a son next year. Sarah laughs to herself, and the LORD asks if anything is too hard for him. The men look toward Sodom. The LORD tells Abraham that the outcry against Sodom is great. Abraham asks if God will kill the righteous with the wicked. He bargains from fifty down, and the LORD will spare the city for ten.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Abraham pleads for other people’s lives. He says the Judge of all the earth should do right (verse 25). For whom is he asking?

contextNote.title: Abraham questions judgment through its effect on others
contextNote.text: Verse 19 says God chose Abraham to teach “righteousness and justice.” Verses 17–21 then let him hear the plan for Sodom. Abraham uses those same two ideas in verse 25. He does not ask God to ignore the wicked. He asks that the righteous not be treated like them. He calls God “the Judge of all the earth” and holds him to that. Each of six requests gets a yes, down to ten people (verse 32).

passages.title: Sodom and Lot's escape
passages.summary: Two angels come to Sodom, and Lot urges them to stay in his house. The men of the city surround it and demand the guests. Lot offers his two daughters, and the crowd turns on him. The angels pull Lot in and strike the men blind. They warn that the LORD will destroy the city, but Lot’s sons-in-law think he jokes. At dawn the angels drag Lot, his wife, and his daughters out. Fire and sulfur fall, and Lot’s wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. In a cave, Lot’s daughters make him drunk and bear Moab and Ben Ammi.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Lot lingers even after the warning (verse 16). What does the verse say made the angels take his hand?

contextNote.title: Hospitality exposes a grave conflict over protection
contextNote.text: Lot takes the guests in and tries to protect them. His way of doing it is to offer his daughters (verse 8). The text reports this without praise. His reason is that the men are “under the shadow of my roof.” He guards guests and gives up the people who most depend on him. The angels, not Lot, save everyone in the house (verses 10–11). Verse 29 says Lot was spared because God remembered Abraham.

passages.title: Abraham and Abimelech
passages.summary: Abraham moves to Gerar and again says Sarah is his sister. King Abimelech takes her. God warns Abimelech in a dream that she is a man’s wife. Abimelech says he acted with a clean heart, and God agrees. In the morning he asks Abraham why he did this. Abraham says he thought no one there feared God. He adds that Sarah is his half sister. Abimelech gives animals, servants, and silver, and Abraham prays for his house.

lds.text: Abraham’s fear puts Sarah at risk. He assumed no one in Gerar feared God (verse 11). What do verses 4–8 show about Abimelech?

contextNote.title: Abraham's fear misjudges the people around him
contextNote.text: Abraham explains himself in verse 11 with a guess about Gerar. He thought no one there feared God. The chapter has already shown the guess was wrong. Abimelech pleads his innocence, and God accepts it (verses 5–6). His servants are “very scared” when they hear (verse 8). The foreign king acts with more care than the prophet. Still, verse 7 has Abraham pray for him, and verse 17 says God heals.

passages.title: Isaac and Ishmael
passages.summary: The LORD does as he said, and Sarah bears Isaac when Abraham is one hundred. Sarah says God has made her laugh. At Isaac’s weaning feast, Sarah sees Hagar’s son mocking. She tells Abraham to send Hagar and the boy away. Abraham is grieved, but God says to listen and promises a nation from the boy. In the wilderness the water runs out, and Hagar weeps. God hears the boy, and Hagar sees a well. Abraham and Abimelech then swear an oath over a well at Beersheba.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: God hears Hagar and Ishmael. Verse 17 says God heard the boy “where he is.” What does Hagar see in verse 19?

contextNote.title: Water answers exclusion with a means to survive
contextNote.text: Hagar leaves with bread and one container of water (verse 14). When it is empty she sits apart so she will not watch her son die. Verse 17 says twice that God heard the boy. The help in verse 19 is small and exact: she sees a well. The text does not say a well was made. It says her eyes were opened. Verse 20 adds what lasts: God was with the boy as he grew.

passages.title: The binding of Isaac
passages.summary: God tests Abraham and tells him to offer his son Isaac in Moriah. Abraham rises early and travels three days with Isaac and two servants. Isaac carries the wood and asks where the lamb is. Abraham says God will provide the lamb. He builds the altar, binds Isaac, and takes the knife. The LORD’s angel stops him and says he now knows Abraham fears God. Abraham offers a ram caught in a thicket. The LORD swears to bless him and all nations through his offspring.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Jacob 4:5 links Abraham’s offering with the Father’s gift of Christ. Genesis itself stops Isaac’s sacrifice. Isaac asks where the lamb is (verse 7). How does his father answer in verse 8?

contextNote.title: The reader knows something Isaac does not
contextNote.text: Verse 1 tells the reader this is a test. Abraham and Isaac are not told. So Isaac’s question in verse 7 is asked in the dark. Abraham’s answer in verse 8 is all he has: “God will provide.” The line “they both went together” comes before and after it (verses 6 and 8). Verse 13 gives the ram, and verse 14 names the place for that answer. The promise in verses 16–18 repeats 12:3 with an oath added.

passages.title: Sarah's burial
passages.summary: Sarah dies at Hebron at age 127, and Abraham mourns her. He tells the Hittites he is a foreigner and asks for a burial place. They offer him the best of their tombs. Abraham asks to buy the cave of Machpelah from Ephron at full price. Ephron offers the field as a gift, then names its worth: four hundred shekels. Abraham weighs out the silver before the people at the city gate. The field, cave, and trees are deeded to him. He buries Sarah there.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Abraham secures a burial place for Sarah. He calls himself “a stranger and a foreigner” (verse 4). Why does he insist on paying in verse 13?

contextNote.title: A grave becomes a claim to land
contextNote.text: God promised Abraham this land in 12:7 and 13:15. Yet in verse 4 he owns none of it and calls himself a foreigner. He is offered a free tomb twice and refuses both times. He wants a purchase made before witnesses (verses 13 and 16). Verses 17–18 read like a deed: field, cave, trees, borders, and witnesses. A grave is the first piece of the promised land he owns. A cuneiform tablet shows how another people recorded a field sale.

passages.title: Rebekah meets Isaac
passages.summary: Old Abraham makes his servant swear to find Isaac a wife among his relatives. The servant takes ten camels to the city of Nahor. At the well he prays for a woman who also waters his camels. Rebekah comes and does just that. He gives her gold and learns she is Bethuel’s daughter, of Abraham’s family. He tells her brother Laban the whole story, and the family agrees. They ask Rebekah, and she says, “I will go.” Isaac meets her, marries her, and loves her.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Rebekah agrees to the journey. Her family asks if she will go with the servant (verse 58). What had Abraham said about an unwilling woman in verse 8?

contextNote.title: Rebekah's answer matters within a family arrangement
contextNote.text: The marriage is arranged by others for most of the chapter. Abraham sends, the servant prays, and Laban and Bethuel agree (verse 51). Yet verse 8 made the woman’s willingness a condition from the start. In verse 57 the family says, “We will call the young lady, and ask her.” Her answer in verse 58 is three words: “I will go.” Like Abram in 12:1, she leaves her family for a land unseen. Verse 60 gives her a blessing close to Abraham’s in 22:17.

passages.title: Abraham's death and the twins
passages.summary: Abraham marries Keturah and has more sons, but he gives all he has to Isaac. He dies at 175, and Isaac and Ishmael bury him beside Sarah. Ishmael’s twelve sons are listed. Isaac prays for Rebekah, who has no child, and she conceives twins. The LORD tells her the elder will serve the younger. Esau is born first, red and hairy, and Jacob follows holding his heel. Esau comes in from the field starving and asks for Jacob’s stew. Jacob asks for the birthright, and Esau swears it away.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: The birthright concerns a lasting family responsibility. Esau asks what good the birthright is to him (verse 32). What does verse 34 say about his choice?

contextNote.title: Immediate need changes how Esau values inheritance
contextNote.text: The birthright is the firstborn’s share, and its benefit lies in the future. Esau’s hunger is now. In verse 32 he says he will die, so the birthright is worthless. Jacob does not offer food first. He asks for a sale and then an oath (verses 31 and 33). Verse 34 lists Esau’s acts quickly: he ate, drank, rose, and left. The writer then gives a verdict: Esau “despised his birthright.”

passages.title: Isaac's wells
passages.summary: In a famine the LORD tells Isaac to stay and not go to Egypt. He repeats to Isaac the oath he swore to Abraham. In Gerar Isaac says Rebekah is his sister, and Abimelech finds out and rebukes him. Isaac’s crops yield a hundredfold, and the Philistines envy him. They fill his father’s wells with earth and send him away. Isaac’s men dig wells, and the herdsmen of Gerar claim two of them. He moves again, digs a third, and names it Rehoboth for the room they found. Abimelech then comes to make a peace oath at Beersheba.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Genesis names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: God renews the promise to Isaac. Isaac gives up two wells without a fight (verses 20–21). What does he say at the third well in verse 22?

contextNote.title: Moving away changes the struggle over water
contextNote.text: Water is life for herds, so each well is worth a fight. Isaac’s men dig, and others claim the water twice. He names the wells for the quarrels and moves on (verses 20–21). The third well brings no dispute, and he credits the LORD with making room. Verse 16 says he was the stronger party, so he was not forced by weakness. Verse 28 shows the result: his rivals come to him asking for peace. They say they saw that the LORD was with him.

passages.title: Jacob receives the blessing
passages.summary: Isaac is old and blind and sends Esau to hunt game before he blesses him. Rebekah hears and tells Jacob to bring two goats. She dresses Jacob in Esau’s clothes and covers his hands with goat skins. Jacob tells his father he is Esau. Isaac doubts the voice, feels the hands, and blesses him as lord over his brothers. Esau returns, and Isaac trembles. Esau weeps and begs for a blessing, and plans to kill Jacob. Rebekah tells Jacob to flee to her brother Laban in Haran.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Esau asks his father for a blessing too (verse 38). What does Isaac say he has already given away in verse 37?

contextNote.title: A spoken blessing creates competing claims
contextNote.text: Isaac learns he was tricked, yet he does not take the blessing back. In verse 33 he says of Jacob, “Yes, he will be blessed.” Verse 37 lists what was given: rule, servants, grain, and wine. The spoken words are treated as done and cannot be shared out again. So Esau’s loss is real, and the text records his bitter cry (verse 34). Jacob gains the blessing and loses his home in the same chapter. Verse 45 shows Rebekah’s fear: losing both sons in one day.

passages.title: Jacob's dream at Bethel
passages.summary: Isaac blesses Jacob and sends him to Paddan Aram to marry a daughter of Laban. Esau sees this and marries a daughter of Ishmael. On the way Jacob sleeps with a stone under his head. He dreams of a stairway to heaven with angels going up and down. The LORD promises him the land, many offspring, and his presence everywhere. Jacob wakes and says the LORD is in this place. He sets up the stone, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel. He vows a tenth to God if God brings him home in peace.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: God meets Jacob while he travels away from home. Jacob says, “The LORD is in this place, and I didn’t know it” (verse 16). What had the LORD just promised in verse 15?

contextNote.title: A place becomes sacred during a flight
contextNote.text: Jacob is running from Esau and has only a stone for a pillow (verse 11). God speaks first. He says, “I am with you, and will keep you, wherever you go.” Jacob’s words in verse 16 show surprise. He had not known God was there. He names the spot Bethel and calls it “God’s house” (verses 17–19). His vow in verses 20–22 still begins with “If.”

passages.title: Leah and Rachel
passages.summary: Jacob reaches a well near Haran and meets Rachel, Laban’s daughter. He rolls the stone away, waters her sheep, and weeps. Laban welcomes him as family. Jacob loves Rachel and works seven years for her. At the wedding feast Laban brings him Leah in the evening. Jacob protests, and Laban says the younger is not given before the firstborn. Jacob marries Rachel a week later and works seven more years. The LORD sees that Leah is unloved, and she bears Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: God sees Leah’s pain. Jacob asks Laban why he deceived him (verse 25). Whom had Jacob deceived in chapter 27?

contextNote.title: Deception returns through marriage and labor
contextNote.text: Jacob’s complaint in verse 25 uses the word “deceived.” Isaac used the same idea of Jacob in 27:35. There the younger son took the place of the firstborn. Here Laban puts the firstborn in the place of the younger. His answer in verse 26 names that very rule. Jacob, who tricked a blind father, is tricked at night. The cost falls on Leah as well, whom verse 31 calls “hated.”

passages.title: Jacob's growing household
passages.summary: Rachel has no children and envies Leah. She gives her servant Bilhah to Jacob, and Bilhah bears Dan and Naphtali. Leah gives her servant Zilpah, who bears Gad and Asher. Rachel trades a night with Jacob for Leah’s mandrake plants. Leah bears Issachar, Zebulun, and a daughter, Dinah. God remembers Rachel, and she bears Joseph. Jacob asks to go home, and Laban asks him to stay for wages. Jacob takes the spotted and dark animals as pay, and his flocks grow large.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: The children’s names reveal hope and distress. Leah says Rachel has “taken away my husband” (verse 15). What do the two sisters trade?

contextNote.title: Competition turns intimate relationships into bargaining
contextNote.text: Each sister has what the other wants. Leah has sons, and Rachel has Jacob’s love (29:30–31). In verse 15 they bargain: mandrakes for a night with their husband. Leah then tells Jacob, “I have surely hired you” (verse 16). Talk of hire and wages runs from sons to sheep (verses 18, 28, 32). People in this house are paid for and traded. Yet verses 17 and 22 say God listened to each woman in turn.

passages.title: Jacob leaves Laban
passages.summary: Laban’s sons say Jacob took their father’s wealth, and Laban’s face turns cold. The LORD tells Jacob to return home. Jacob tells Rachel and Leah that Laban changed his wages ten times. They agree to go, saying their father sold them. Jacob leaves in secret, and Rachel steals her father’s household idols. Laban chases them, but God warns him in a dream. He searches the tents and finds nothing, and Jacob lists twenty years of hard service. The two men pile stones as a border and swear to do no harm.

lds.text: Jacob and Laban set a boundary. Rachel and Leah say their father “has sold us” (verse 15). What do they tell Jacob to do in verse 16?

contextNote.title: The daughters explain the cost of their father's control
contextNote.text: Jacob asks his wives before he leaves, and verses 14–16 give their answer. They speak together, though they were rivals in chapter 30. They say their father treats them as foreigners. He “sold” them and used up the money. Jacob worked fourteen years for them (verse 41). So they count the flocks God gave Jacob as rightly theirs and their children’s. Their consent turns Jacob’s flight into a family decision.

passages.title: Jacob wrestles
passages.summary: Angels meet Jacob on his way. He sends word to Esau, and hears that Esau is coming with four hundred men. Jacob is afraid and splits his camp in two. He prays, saying he is not worthy, and asks God to save him from Esau. He sends herds ahead as a gift, with space between them. That night he sends his family across the Jabbok and is left alone. A man wrestles with him until dawn and strains his hip. The man names him Israel, and Jacob limps away from Peniel.

lds.text: Jacob receives the name Israel after a struggle. Jacob tells God, “I fear him” (verse 11). What promise does he remind God of in verse 12?

contextNote.title: Prayer names a fear that preparation cannot remove
contextNote.text: Jacob plans first: two camps, so one may escape (verses 7–8). Then he prays. Verse 11 is plain about the fear and names who could die: mothers and children. He bases the request on God’s own words (verses 9 and 12). He claims nothing for himself and says he is “not worthy” (verse 10). After the prayer he still sends gifts. The chapter shows planning and prayer together, and neither removes the fear.

passages.title: Jacob and Esau meet
passages.summary: Jacob sees Esau coming with four hundred men. He lines up the women and children and goes ahead, bowing seven times. Esau runs to him, hugs him, and they weep. Esau asks about the family and about the herds he met. Esau says he has enough, but Jacob urges him to take the gift. Esau offers to travel together, but Jacob says his children and flocks are slow. Esau returns to Seir. Jacob goes to Succoth and then Shechem, buys land, and builds an altar.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Esau welcomes Jacob. Jacob says seeing Esau’s face is like seeing “the face of God” (verse 10). What did Esau do in verse 4?

contextNote.title: An embrace interrupts the expected account of revenge
contextNote.text: Jacob expected an attack and arranged his family for one (verses 1–2). Verse 4 gives five quick acts: ran, embraced, fell on his neck, kissed, wept. Jacob had just named a place Peniel for seeing God’s face and living (32:30). In verse 10 he says the same of Esau’s face. He expected judgment from both and was spared by both. He urges Esau to accept the gift, and Esau does (verse 11).

passages.title: Dinah and Shechem
passages.summary: Dinah, Leah’s daughter, goes out to visit the women of the land. Shechem, the prince’s son, takes her, lies with her, and shames her. He then wants to marry her, and his father Hamor asks Jacob. Jacob’s sons answer with deceit: every male in the city must be circumcised. On the third day Simeon and Levi kill all the males and take Dinah back. The brothers plunder the city and take the women and children. Jacob says they have put the family in danger. They ask if their sister should be treated like a prostitute.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Dinah suffers violence and her brothers take revenge. The chapter ends with a question (verse 31). Who in the chapter never gets to speak?

contextNote.title: The final question leaves responsibility unresolved
contextNote.text: The chapter gives Dinah no words. Shechem, Hamor, Jacob, and her brothers all speak about her. Jacob’s complaint in verse 30 is about his own safety among the neighbors. The brothers’ answer in verse 31 is about their sister’s honor. Neither answer settles the matter, and the chapter stops on their question. The brothers used the covenant sign as a weapon (verses 13–15 and 25). In 49:5–7 Jacob curses the anger of Simeon and Levi.

passages.title: Return to Bethel
passages.summary: God tells Jacob to go up to Bethel and build an altar. Jacob tells his household to put away foreign gods and make themselves clean. They hand over the gods and earrings, and he buries them under an oak. At Bethel God blesses him, repeats the name Israel, and promises the land. Rebekah’s nurse Deborah dies there. On the road Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin and is buried near Bethlehem. Reuben lies with Bilhah, his father’s concubine. Jacob reaches Isaac at Hebron, and Esau and Jacob bury their father.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Jacob returns to worship amid family loss. Before going to Bethel, Jacob gives three orders (verse 2). What must the household put away?

contextNote.title: Returning to worship requires a household decision
contextNote.text: God’s order in verse 1 is to Jacob alone: go, live there, build an altar. Jacob turns it into orders for everyone with him (verse 2). The first is to give up foreign gods. Rachel had taken her father’s idols in 31:19. So the journey to Bethel begins by clearing the camp. Verse 3 gives Jacob’s reason: God answered him in distress and stayed with him. That is the promise of 28:15, now reported as kept.

passages.title: Esau's descendants
passages.summary: This is the family record of Esau, who is also called Edom. Esau’s wives bear him five sons in Canaan. He moves to Seir, because the land cannot hold both brothers’ herds. His sons and grandsons become chiefs of Edom. The Horites, who lived in Seir, are listed with their chiefs. Eight kings rule Edom before Israel has any king. No king in the list is the son of the king before him. The list ends with Esau as the father of the Edomites.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Esau’s descendants have their own place in Genesis. Verse 31 says Edom had kings before Israel did. Why might Genesis keep a careful record of Esau’s family?

contextNote.title: Israel's neighbor has a history beyond its role as a rival
contextNote.text: Esau lost the blessing, yet Genesis gives his family a full chapter. Verse 7 repeats the reason Abram and Lot parted: too many herds (13:6). So the brothers separate without a fight. Verse 31 notes that Edom had kings before Israel had one. Kings were promised to Jacob in 35:11, yet Esau’s line has them first. The chapter treats Edom as a real people with land, chiefs, and rulers. Deuteronomy 2:4–5 later says God gave Seir to Esau.

passages.title: Joseph sold
passages.summary: Israel loves seventeen-year-old Joseph most and gives him a tunic of many colors. His brothers hate him more when he dreams that they bow to him. Jacob sends Joseph to check on his brothers near Shechem. They plan to kill him, but Reuben persuades them to throw him in a pit. Judah proposes selling him, and he is sold for twenty pieces of silver. The brothers dip his tunic in goat’s blood and show it to their father. Jacob decides an animal killed Joseph and refuses comfort. In Egypt Joseph is sold to Potiphar, Pharaoh’s captain of the guard.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Joseph loses home through his brothers’ choices. The brothers ask Jacob to “examine” the tunic (verse 32). Who used goat skins to trick a father in chapter 27?

contextNote.title: A garment becomes false evidence for a grieving father
contextNote.text: The brothers never say Joseph is dead. In verse 32 they hand over the tunic and ask their father to examine it. Jacob supplies the false story himself in verse 33. The tunic was the sign of his favor in verse 3. Now it is the proof of his loss. Jacob once deceived his father with goat skins and a brother’s clothes (27:15–16). Here a goat’s blood and a son’s clothes deceive him.

passages.title: Judah and Tamar
passages.summary: Judah marries a Canaanite woman and has three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah. Er marries Tamar and dies. Onan refuses to give his brother an heir and also dies. Judah sends Tamar home and keeps Shelah from her. Later Tamar veils herself by the road, and Judah takes her for a prostitute. He leaves his signet, cord, and staff as a pledge, and she conceives. When Judah hears she is pregnant, he orders her burned. She sends him the pledge, and he says she is more righteous than he.

lds.text: Judah admits that Tamar has a stronger claim. Judah says, “She is more righteous than I” (verse 26). What reason does he give?

contextNote.title: Judah's admission reverses his judgment of Tamar
contextNote.text: Judah’s duty was to give Tamar his third son, as verse 8 explains for Onan. Verse 11 shows he held Shelah back out of fear. Verse 14 says Tamar acted when she saw she had been passed over. Judah condemns her at once in verse 24, without a hearing. Her message in verse 25 says, “Please discern whose these are.” The brothers asked Jacob to examine Joseph’s tunic in the same way (37:32). This time Judah tells the truth and names his own fault.

passages.title: Joseph in Potiphar's house
passages.summary: Potiphar, an Egyptian officer, buys Joseph. The LORD is with Joseph, and Potiphar puts him over his whole house. Potiphar’s wife asks Joseph to lie with her, and he refuses. He says it would wrong his master and be a sin against God. One day she grabs his garment, and he runs out and leaves it. She tells the household and her husband that the Hebrew servant came at her. Potiphar puts Joseph in the king’s prison. The LORD is with him there, and the keeper puts him over the prisoners.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Joseph refuses sexual wrongdoing and faces a false charge. What two reasons does he give for refusing in verses 8–9?

contextNote.title: A master's household controls whose account gains force
contextNote.text: Joseph’s garment is used against him for the second time (37:31–33). His master’s wife holds it and tells the story first. She tells it twice and changes it for each hearer. To the servants she blames her husband for bringing “a Hebrew” (verse 14). To her husband she says “the Hebrew servant, whom you have brought” (verse 17). The text records no answer from Joseph, a slave. Verse 21 repeats what verse 2 said: the LORD was with Joseph.

passages.title: Dreams in prison
passages.summary: Pharaoh’s chief cup bearer and chief baker are jailed where Joseph is held. Joseph looks after them. Each has a dream on the same night, and Joseph sees they are sad. He says interpretations belong to God and asks to hear the dreams. He tells the cup bearer he will get his post back in three days. He asks the cup bearer to remember him and speak to Pharaoh. He tells the baker he will be hanged in three days. Both things happen on Pharaoh’s birthday, and the cup bearer forgets Joseph.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Joseph serves others while he waits in prison. He asks the cup bearer to “remember me” (verse 14). What does verse 23 say happened?

contextNote.title: Help depends on being remembered by someone with access
contextNote.text: Joseph gives the meaning of the dream without asking for pay. Then verse 14 makes one request: “remember me.” A prisoner cannot reach Pharaoh, but the cup bearer hands him his cup. In verse 15 Joseph states his case in two parts. He was stolen from his land, and he did nothing to earn the dungeon. Verse 23 answers with two verbs: he did not remember, he forgot. Chapter 41:1 says two full years pass.

passages.title: Joseph before Pharaoh
passages.summary: Two years later Pharaoh dreams of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones. He also dreams of seven good heads of grain swallowed by seven thin ones. No wise man can explain it, and the cup bearer remembers Joseph. Joseph says the answer is not in him but comes from God. The dreams mean seven years of plenty and then seven of famine. He advises storing a fifth of each harvest under a wise man. Pharaoh sets Joseph over all Egypt and gives him his ring and a wife. Joseph stores grain, has two sons, and sells grain when the famine comes.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Joseph prepares for famine after explaining the dreams. He tells Pharaoh the answer is not in him (verse 16). What plan does he give in verses 33–36?

contextNote.title: Food storage creates political power
contextNote.text: Pharaoh asked for a meaning, and Joseph adds a plan (verses 33–36). The plan is practical: overseers, a fifth of each harvest, and stores in the cities. Verse 36 states its purpose: “that the land will not perish.” The stored grain is held “under the hand of Pharaoh” (verse 35). So saving lives and growing the king’s power arrive together. Chapter 47 shows what that power later costs the people. An Egyptian granary model shows scribes recording grain, as a comparison only.

passages.title: The brothers seek grain
passages.summary: Jacob sends ten sons to Egypt for grain but keeps Benjamin home. They bow before Joseph, the governor, and do not know him. Joseph knows them, remembers his dreams, and calls them spies. He holds them three days, then keeps Simeon and demands Benjamin. The brothers say to each other that they are guilty about Joseph. Joseph understands them and turns away to weep. He fills their sacks and puts their money back in them. Back home, Jacob refuses to let Benjamin go.

lds.text: The brothers begin to acknowledge their earlier harm. They say, “We are certainly guilty concerning our brother” (verse 21). What do they remember Joseph doing in the pit?

contextNote.title: The brothers supply a past explanation for a present threat
contextNote.text: Joseph accuses the brothers of spying, which they did not do. Their minds go straight to something else. Verse 21 is the first time they call themselves guilty about Joseph. It adds a detail chapter 37 left out: he begged, and they would not listen. They link their distress now to his distress then. They speak freely, thinking the governor cannot understand (verse 23). Verse 24 shows he hears every word and weeps.

passages.title: Benjamin goes to Egypt
passages.summary: The grain runs out, and Jacob tells his sons to buy more. Judah says they cannot go without Benjamin. He offers himself as a pledge for the boy’s return. Israel agrees and sends gifts and double money. In Egypt, Joseph has the brothers brought to his house, and they fear a trap. The steward calms them and brings Simeon out. Joseph sees Benjamin, leaves the room, and weeps. The brothers are seated by age, and Benjamin gets five times as much food.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Judah accepts responsibility for Benjamin. He tells his father, “I’ll be collateral for him” (verse 9). How does that differ from his plan for Joseph in 37:26–27?

contextNote.title: Judah makes another person's safety his own responsibility
contextNote.text: Reuben offered his two sons’ lives as a pledge in 42:37, and Jacob refused. Judah offers himself in verse 9. He does not promise that nothing will go wrong. He promises to carry the blame “forever” if it does. In 37:26–27 Judah was the one who proposed selling Joseph. Verse 8 gives his reason now: so that the whole family may live. Jacob accepts in verses 11–14 and lets Benjamin go.

passages.title: Judah offers himself
passages.summary: Joseph has his silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s sack. His steward overtakes the brothers and finds it there. They tear their clothes and all return to the city. Judah says God has found out their guilt, and all will be slaves. Joseph says only the one with the cup will stay. Judah steps close and tells of their old father and his love for the boy. He says the father will die if Benjamin does not return. He asks to stay as a slave in the boy’s place.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Judah offers his own freedom for Benjamin. He asks to stay “instead of the boy” (verse 33). Whose pain does he want to prevent in verse 34?

contextNote.title: Judah answers the test by accepting another person's loss
contextNote.text: Joseph’s test repeats the old choice. They may leave Rachel’s favored son as a slave and go home (verse 17). In chapter 37 the brothers took that way out. This time they all return together (verse 13). Judah’s speech quotes their father’s love for Benjamin without anger (verses 27–31). Verse 33 offers a trade: Judah’s freedom for the boy’s. Verse 34 gives his reason, which is his father’s grief.

passages.title: Joseph reveals himself
passages.summary: Joseph can no longer hold back and sends everyone else out. He weeps aloud and says, “I am Joseph!” His brothers are too afraid to answer. He says not to be angry, because God sent him ahead to save lives. Five years of famine remain, so they must bring his father to Goshen. He weeps on Benjamin and kisses all his brothers. Pharaoh sends wagons and promises the best of Egypt. Jacob’s heart faints at the news, then revives when he sees the wagons.

lds.text: Joseph speaks truth about the sale while preserving the family. He says both “you sold me” and “God sent me” (verse 5). How can both be true?

contextNote.title: Joseph separates the wrong from its later outcome
contextNote.text: Joseph does not hide what his brothers did. Verse 4 says “whom you sold,” and verse 5 says “you sold me here.” In the same sentence he says “God sent me.” He names the purpose twice: to preserve life (verses 5 and 7). The sale was their act, and the rescue was God’s use of it. Verse 8 goes furthest: “it wasn’t you who sent me here, but God.” Joseph says this after Judah’s offer in 44:33 showed the brothers had changed.

passages.title: Jacob goes to Egypt
passages.summary: Israel sets out and offers sacrifices at Beersheba. God tells him in a night vision not to fear going to Egypt. God will make him a great nation there and bring him back. Jacob’s sons carry him, their wives, and their children in Pharaoh’s wagons. The chapter lists the family by mother, seventy people in all. Judah goes ahead to lead the way to Goshen. Joseph meets his father and weeps on his neck for a long time. He tells his brothers to say they are herdsmen, so they can live in Goshen.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: God reassures Jacob before the move to Egypt. God says, “I will go down with you into Egypt” (verse 4). What else does he promise in that verse?

contextNote.title: An outsider identity shapes where the family can settle
contextNote.text: Joseph coaches his brothers on one answer for Pharaoh: they keep livestock. Verse 34 gives the reason. Egyptians look down on shepherds, so the family will be settled apart in Goshen. The low standing of their trade becomes their protection. Living apart, they can stay one family. God’s promise in verse 3 is that they will become a nation there. Verse 4 adds that he will bring them up again.

passages.title: The famine continues
passages.summary: Joseph presents five brothers to Pharaoh, and they ask to live in Goshen as shepherds. Pharaoh gives them the best of the land. Jacob, age 130, blesses Pharaoh and calls his years few and hard. The famine grows worse. The Egyptians pay Joseph for grain with money, then with livestock. In the end they sell their land and themselves to Pharaoh. Joseph gives them seed and takes a fifth of each harvest for Pharaoh. Before he dies, Israel makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Joseph gives people food, but they lose land and freedom. The people say Joseph saved their lives (verse 25). What did they give up in verses 19–20?

contextNote.title: Relief brings survival and a new claim on labor
contextNote.text: The famine takes the Egyptians’ money, livestock, land, and labor in turn (verses 14–20). The people propose the last step themselves in verse 19. Joseph accepts it for Pharaoh, not for himself. Verse 23 states the new fact plainly: “I have bought you and your land.” He also gives seed and leaves them four fifths of the crop (verse 24). The people call it rescue (verse 25), yet they become Pharaoh’s servants. The Egyptian granary model shows scribes recording stored grain.

passages.title: Ephraim and Manasseh
passages.summary: Joseph hears his father is sick and brings his sons Manasseh and Ephraim. Jacob recalls God’s promise at Luz and claims the two boys as his own sons. He remembers Rachel’s death on the road. Israel’s eyes are dim, and he kisses the boys. Joseph sets Manasseh, the firstborn, at Israel’s right hand. Israel crosses his hands and puts his right hand on Ephraim. Joseph objects, and his father says, “I know, my son, I know.” He sets Ephraim before Manasseh and promises that God will bring them back.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Jacob blesses both sons and gives Ephraim the leading place. Joseph says, “Not so, my father” (verse 18). How does Jacob answer in verse 19?

contextNote.title: An expected order becomes a deliberate choice
contextNote.text: Joseph arranges the boys so the firstborn gets the right hand (verse 13). Jacob crosses his hands “knowingly” (verse 14). Joseph thinks his blind father has made a mistake and moves the hand. Verse 19 answers twice: “I know, my son, I know.” Jacob was himself a younger son who received the first place (chapter 27). Then a blind father was tricked. Here a blind father chooses on purpose and blesses both boys.

passages.title: Jacob's final words
passages.summary: Jacob gathers his sons to tell what will come to each. Reuben, the firstborn, will not excel, because he went to his father’s bed. Simeon and Levi are cursed for their anger and will be scattered. Judah is a lion’s cub, and the ruler’s staff will stay with him. Zebulun, Issachar, Dan, Gad, Asher, and Naphtali each get a short saying. Joseph is a fruitful vine, helped by the Mighty One of Jacob. Benjamin is a hungry wolf. Jacob orders his burial in the cave at Machpelah and dies.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Jacob’s words join blessing with consequences. He curses the anger of Simeon and Levi, not the men (verse 7). What event in chapter 34 does verse 6 recall?

contextNote.title: Blessing can include criticism of the family's past
contextNote.text: Verse 28 calls all of these sayings blessings. Yet the first three sons hear about their past. Reuben is told of his father’s bed (35:22). Simeon and Levi are told of the men they killed (34:25). In verse 7 Jacob curses their anger and wrath, not their persons. Their penalty is to be scattered among the other tribes. The first place then passes to the fourth son, Judah, in verses 8–10.

passages.title: Burial and forgiveness
passages.summary: Joseph weeps over his father and has him embalmed. Egypt mourns seventy days. With Pharaoh’s leave, Joseph and a great company bury Jacob in the cave at Machpelah. Back in Egypt the brothers fear that Joseph will now repay them. They send a message asking forgiveness and bow before him. Joseph weeps and tells them not to fear. He says they meant evil, but God meant it for good, to save many lives. Dying at 110, he makes Israel swear to carry his bones out of Egypt.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Second Nephi 3 adds Joseph’s prophecy about a future seer. The brothers fear payback after their father dies (verse 15). What question does Joseph ask in verse 19?

contextNote.title: Reconciliation must continue after the father's death
contextNote.text: Seventeen years have passed since Joseph forgave his brothers (45:5; 47:28). Verse 15 shows they still fear him once their father is gone. They offer to be his slaves in verse 18. Joseph answers with a question: “Am I in the place of God?” He will not take the judge’s seat. Verse 20 keeps both truths from chapter 45: they meant evil, and God meant good. Verse 21 turns forgiveness into a promise to feed them and their children.

events.title: Creation
events.summary: In the beginning God creates the heavens and the earth. He speaks, and light, sky, land, and plants appear over three days. Sun, moon, stars, sea animals, and birds follow. On the sixth day he makes land animals and then people. He makes people in his own image, male and female. He blesses them and tells them to fill the earth and rule the animals. He gives plants as food to people and animals. God sees all he has made and calls it very good.
events.detail: Six times the chapter says God saw that his work was good. People come last, and verse 31 says “very good.” Verse 27 says “image” twice and then names both male and female. No one group holds that standing alone. The command to rule in verse 28 comes after the blessing. Verses 29–30 then give plants as food to people and animals alike. So ruling here sits beside care for life that God called good.
events.uncertainty: The map has no sure location for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 2 places human creation within God’s work. Verse 27 says God made male and female in his image. How should that shape the way you treat people?

events.title: Life in the garden
events.summary: God finishes his work, rests on the seventh day, and makes that day holy. Then the LORD God forms a man from dust and breathes life into him. God plants a garden in Eden with a river and two named trees. He puts the man there to work it and keep it. He forbids one tree and warns of death. God says it is not good for the man to be alone. The man names the animals, but none is a helper like him. God makes a woman from his rib, and the man welcomes her as his flesh.
events.detail: Chapter 1 said “good” again and again. Verse 18 is the first “not good.” The man already has a garden, food, and work (verses 15–16). In verses 19–20 he meets every animal and names it. Naming shows he knows them, yet none is “comparable to him.” Only then does God make the woman. The man’s words in verse 23 are about likeness: bone of his bones.
events.uncertainty: The map has no sure location for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 3 connects the garden with God’s commands. The man has work and food but is alone (verse 18). What need does the woman answer in verse 23?

events.title: The Fall
events.summary: The serpent asks the woman what God really said. She repeats the command, and the serpent says she will not die. She sees the fruit is good, eats, and gives some to her husband. Their eyes open, and they cover themselves and hide. God asks where the man is and whether he ate. The man blames the woman, and the woman blames the serpent. God curses the serpent and the ground, and speaks of pain and hard work. He clothes them with skins and sends them out of Eden.
events.detail: God asks the man two direct questions in verses 9 and 11. Verse 12 answers neither one first. The man names the woman, and then names God as the one who gave her. “I ate” comes last. In 2:23 he called her bone of his bones. Now he puts her between himself and God. Verse 13 shows the same move when the woman points to the serpent.
events.uncertainty: The map has no sure location for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 4 expands the garden account. Second Nephi 2 connects the Fall with choice and redemption. The man answers God by blaming two others (verse 12). Whom does he blame?

events.title: Cain and Abel
events.summary: Eve bears Cain and then Abel. Cain farms, and Abel keeps sheep. Both bring offerings, and the LORD accepts Abel’s but not Cain’s. The LORD warns Cain that sin crouches at the door. Cain kills Abel in the field and asks if he is his brother’s keeper. The LORD sends Cain away as a wanderer but marks him for protection. Cain’s family builds a city, and Lamech boasts of killing a man. Eve bears Seth, and people begin to call on the LORD’s name.
events.detail: Verse 15 sets a limit. God promises sevenfold vengeance to stop anyone from killing Cain. In verse 24 Lamech takes that promise for himself and multiplies it. He has killed a young man for a wound (verse 23). No one gave him this protection. A rule meant to hold back killing becomes a boast about killing. Verse 26 ends with a different use of speech: calling on the LORD’s name.
events.uncertainty: The map has no sure location for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 5 adds gospel teaching after the Fall. The LORD warns Cain before he kills (verse 7). What does the warning say Cain can still do?

events.title: Generations to Noah
events.summary: This is the family record from Adam to Noah. God made people in his likeness, and Adam fathers Seth in his own likeness. Each entry gives a father’s age, his son, his total years, and his death. The years are very long, up to 969 for Methuselah. Enoch’s entry is different. He walks with God, and God takes him. Lamech names his son Noah and hopes for comfort from the cursed ground. Noah fathers Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
events.detail: The chapter repeats one pattern eight times and ends each with “then he died.” Genesis 2:17 warned of death, and the list shows it arriving. Enoch breaks the pattern in verses 22–24. The text says twice that he “walked with God.” His entry has no death line. It says God took him. Verse 29 adds a second break: a father hopes his son will bring relief.
events.uncertainty: The map has no sure location for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 6–7 expands Enoch’s account. Every entry but one ends with “then he died.” What does verse 24 say about Enoch?

events.title: Noah builds the ark
events.summary: People multiply, and God’s sons take human daughters as wives. The LORD says man’s days will be 120 years. He sees that human thoughts are evil all the time, and he is grieved. He decides to wipe out people and animals. But Noah finds favor and walks with God. God tells Noah the earth is filled with violence. He orders a ship of gopher wood with three levels and one door. Noah is to bring his family, pairs of animals, and food, and he obeys.
events.detail: Verse 5 gives the cause of the flood as seen in the human heart. Verse 11 gives it as seen on the ground: violence fills the earth. The word “corrupt” appears three times in verses 11–12. God’s word for what he will do in verse 13 is “destroy.” The earth is already ruined by its people before the water comes. Verse 6 shows the decision costs God grief. Verse 8 keeps one door open: Noah finds favor.

lds.text: Moses 8 describes Noah’s preaching before the flood. Verse 9 says Noah “walked with God.” What does verse 22 say he did with God’s orders?

events.title: The flood
events.summary: The LORD tells Noah to enter the ship with his household. Noah takes seven pairs of clean animals and one pair of the others. Noah is six hundred years old. After seven days the deep bursts open and the sky’s windows open. Rain falls forty days and nights. Noah’s family and the animals go in, and the LORD shuts him in. The water lifts the ship and covers the high mountains. Everything on dry land dies, and only those in the ship remain.
events.detail: Noah builds the ship and loads it, as verses 5 and 9 say. One act is not his: closing the door. Verse 16 says “the LORD shut him in.” Noah’s safety rests on that act, not on his building alone. The closed door keeps the family in and the water out. It also marks the end of the time to enter. Verse 23 states the result: only those inside are left.

lds.text: The Church manual reads Noah’s deliverance within God’s dealings with humanity. Verse 5 says Noah did all the LORD commanded. What does the LORD do for Noah in verse 16?

events.title: The waters recede
events.summary: God remembers Noah and the animals and sends a wind. The water goes down, and the ship rests on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sends out a raven and then a dove. The dove comes back with an olive leaf, then does not return. God tells Noah to leave the ship with his family and the animals. Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings. The LORD says he will not again curse the ground or strike every living thing. Seedtime and harvest, summer and winter, day and night will not stop.
events.detail: Verse 21 gives a surprising reason for the promise. The human heart is still “evil from his youth,” as in 6:5. The flood did not change people. What changes is what God says he will do. Verse 22 puts the promise in farm terms: planting, harvest, cold, heat. People can plan a year because these will come. Noah’s first act on dry ground is an offering, not a field (verse 20).

lds.text: Noah worships after deliverance. Verse 1 says God “remembered Noah.” What does God promise about seasons in verse 22?

events.title: A covenant with Noah
events.summary: God blesses Noah and his sons and tells them to fill the earth. Animals will fear them, and they may eat meat but not blood. God will demand a reckoning for human life, because he made people in his image. He makes a covenant with Noah, his family, and every living creature. No flood will destroy the earth again, and the rainbow is the sign. Noah plants a vineyard and gets drunk. Ham sees his father naked, and Shem and Japheth cover him. Noah curses Canaan and blesses Shem and Japheth.
events.detail: After the flood, people may kill animals for food (verse 3). Verse 5 draws a line at human life. Verse 6 gives the reason: “God made man in his own image.” That is the same ground given for human worth in 1:27. The flood did not remove it. So the rule protects every person, not one family or rank. The earth was “filled with violence” in 6:11, and this rule answers that.

lds.text: A covenant is a sacred agreement. Verse 6 gives a reason not to shed human blood. What is the reason?

events.title: Families and nations
events.summary: This is the family record of Noah’s sons after the flood. Japheth’s line spreads to the coasts and islands. Ham’s line includes Cush, Mizraim, and Canaan. Cush’s son Nimrod is a mighty hunter, and his kingdom begins at Babel. Canaan’s families spread from Sidon toward Gaza. Shem’s line includes Eber, Peleg, and Joktan. Each list ends with families, languages, lands, and nations. From these families the nations spread over the earth.
events.detail: The chapter lists many peoples as one family tree. Peoples who later fight Israel appear in it as relatives. Canaan, Assyria, and the Philistines all have a place (verses 11, 14, 15). The refrain in verses 5, 20, and 31 names families, languages, lands, and nations. So difference in language is treated as normal here. Verse 32 sums it up: all nations come from Noah’s sons. Chapter 11 then tells how the languages divided.

lds.text: The family record joins many peoples to common ancestors. Verse 32 says the nations came from one family. How should that shape the way one nation sees another?

events.title: Babel and Terah's family
events.summary: All people speak one language and settle on a plain in Shinar. They bake bricks and plan a city with a tower to the sky. They want a name for themselves and fear being scattered. The LORD comes down to see, confuses their language, and scatters them. The city is called Babel. Then the record runs from Shem to Terah. Terah fathers Abram, Nahor, and Haran, and Abram’s wife Sarai has no child. Terah leaves Ur for Canaan but settles in Haran and dies there.
events.detail: Verse 4 gives the builders two aims. They want a name, and they want not to be scattered. God had told people to fill the earth in 1:28 and 9:1. The tower should reach the sky, yet the LORD “came down” to see it. They get the very thing they feared: scattering (verse 8). In 12:2 God offers Abram a great name as a gift. The chapter sets a name people grab beside a name God gives.

lds.text: The Church manual contrasts Babel with the covenant family story. The builders want “a name for ourselves” (verse 4). Who promises a great name in 12:2?

events.title: Abram's call
events.summary: The LORD tells Abram to leave his country and his father’s house. He promises a great nation and a blessing for all families through Abram. Abram goes at age seventy-five with Sarai and Lot. In Canaan the LORD promises the land to his offspring, and Abram builds altars. A famine sends him to Egypt. He asks Sarai to say she is his sister, because he fears being killed. Pharaoh takes her and pays Abram well, and the LORD sends plagues. Pharaoh rebukes Abram and sends them away.
events.detail: The promise in verses 2–3 has seven parts and ends outside Abram’s family. All the families of the earth are to be blessed through him. The rest of the chapter tests that at once. In Egypt Abram protects himself with a false story (verse 13). Pharaoh’s house gets plagues, not blessing (verse 17). A foreign king then corrects the man God chose (verses 18–19). The promise stands, but the chapter shows it does not depend on Abram’s good conduct.

events.title: Abram and Lot separate
events.summary: Abram returns from Egypt to Bethel, rich in livestock, silver, and gold. Lot also has flocks, and the land cannot hold both. Their herdsmen quarrel. Abram asks for no strife and offers Lot his choice of land. Lot sees the well-watered Jordan plain and chooses it. He camps near Sodom, whose men are very wicked. The LORD tells Abram to look all around, for the land will be his. Abram moves to the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and builds an altar.
events.detail: Abram is the uncle, and the land was promised to him (12:7). He could choose first. Verse 9 gives the choice to Lot. His stated reason in verse 8 is “we are relatives.” Verse 10 shows Lot choosing by what his eyes see. Verse 13 warns what was near that green plain. After Lot leaves, the LORD tells Abram to look, and gives him all.

events.title: Lot rescued
events.summary: Four kings make war on five kings near the Salt Sea. The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah flee, and the winners take goods, food, and people. They take Lot, who lives in Sodom. Abram leads 318 trained men, attacks by night, and brings everyone back. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine. He blesses Abram, and Abram gives him a tenth. The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods. Abram refuses even a thread, so the king cannot say he made Abram rich.
events.detail: Two kings meet Abram after the battle. Melchizedek blesses him and credits God with the win (verse 20). Abram gives him a tenth. The king of Sodom offers goods, and Abram takes nothing. Verse 23 gives his reason: no king may say, “I have made Abram rich.” A gift from a ruler could become a claim on him. Verse 24 keeps his rule from costing his allies their share.

events.title: God's covenant with Abram
events.summary: The LORD comes to Abram in a vision and says not to fear. Abram says he has no child, and a servant will be his heir. The LORD says his own son will be his heir and shows him the stars. Abram believes, and the LORD counts it as righteousness. Abram asks how he will know the land is his. He cuts animals in half, and a deep sleep and darkness fall on him. The LORD says his offspring will serve in a foreign land four hundred years. A furnace and a torch pass between the pieces, and the LORD makes a covenant.
events.detail: Abram asks for certainty about the land in verse 8. The answer begins with what he must “know for sure.” His family will be foreigners and slaves for four hundred years. Only then will they come out and return. Verse 16 gives a reason for the wait: the Amorites’ wrong “is not yet full.” So God will not remove a people before its time. In verse 17 only the fire passes between the pieces, while Abram sleeps.

lds.text: God’s promise meets Abraham’s fear about an heir. Abram asks how he will know (verse 8). What hard news comes with the answer in verse 13?

events.title: Hagar and Ishmael
events.summary: Sarai has no children and gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram as a wife. Hagar conceives and looks down on Sarai. Sarai blames Abram, and he says Hagar is in her hand. Sarai treats her harshly, and Hagar runs away. The LORD’s angel finds her by a spring and tells her to return. He promises her many offspring and a son named Ishmael, because the LORD heard. Hagar names the LORD “a God who sees.” She bears Ishmael when Abram is eighty-six.
events.detail: Hagar has no say in verses 2–3. Sarai gives her, and Abram takes her. The angel is the first to speak to her by name (verse 8). Verse 9 sends her back under Sarai’s hand, and the text does not soften that. Verses 10–11 then give her a promise like Abram’s: offspring too many to count. Her son’s name is tied to the LORD hearing her suffering. In verse 13 she is the one who gives God a name.

events.title: New names and covenant
events.summary: Abram is ninety-nine when the LORD appears as God Almighty. God makes a covenant: many nations will come from Abram, and Canaan will be theirs. God changes his name to Abraham. Every male in his house, even bought servants, must be circumcised as the sign. Sarai’s name becomes Sarah, and she will bear a son. Abraham laughs and asks that Ishmael might live before God. God says Sarah will bear Isaac, and Ishmael will also become a great nation. Abraham circumcises every male in his house that same day.
events.detail: God speaks for most of the chapter, and Abraham’s part comes at the end. Verse 23 says he acted “in the same day.” The list of who was circumcised is wide. It names Ishmael, those born in the house, and those bought with money. Verse 21 says the covenant line runs through Isaac, not Ishmael. Yet Ishmael receives the sign and his own blessing (verse 20). The sign covers the whole household, not only the heir.
