events.title: Visitors and Abraham's plea
events.summary: The LORD appears to Abraham at Mamre as three men stand near his tent. Abraham runs to meet them and serves bread, a calf, butter, and milk. One says Sarah will have a son next year. Sarah laughs to herself, and the LORD asks if anything is too hard for him. The men look toward Sodom. The LORD tells Abraham that the outcry against Sodom is great. Abraham asks if God will kill the righteous with the wicked. He bargains from fifty down, and the LORD will spare the city for ten.
events.detail: Verse 19 says God chose Abraham to teach “righteousness and justice.” Verses 17–21 then let him hear the plan for Sodom. Abraham uses those same two ideas in verse 25. He does not ask God to ignore the wicked. He asks that the righteous not be treated like them. He calls God “the Judge of all the earth” and holds him to that. Each of six requests gets a yes, down to ten people (verse 32).

events.title: Sodom and Lot's escape
events.summary: Two angels come to Sodom, and Lot urges them to stay in his house. The men of the city surround it and demand the guests. Lot offers his two daughters, and the crowd turns on him. The angels pull Lot in and strike the men blind. They warn that the LORD will destroy the city, but Lot’s sons-in-law think he jokes. At dawn the angels drag Lot, his wife, and his daughters out. Fire and sulfur fall, and Lot’s wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. In a cave, Lot’s daughters make him drunk and bear Moab and Ben Ammi.
events.detail: Lot takes the guests in and tries to protect them. His way of doing it is to offer his daughters (verse 8). The text reports this without praise. His reason is that the men are “under the shadow of my roof.” He guards guests and gives up the people who most depend on him. The angels, not Lot, save everyone in the house (verses 10–11). Verse 29 says Lot was spared because God remembered Abraham.

events.title: Abraham and Abimelech

Abimelech gives animals, servants, and silver, and Abraham prays for his house.

Abimelech pleads his innocence, and God accepts it (verses 5–6). His servants are “very scared” when they hear (verse 8). The foreign king acts with more care than the prophet. Still, verse 7 has Abraham pray for him, and verse 17 says God heals.

events.title: Isaac and Ishmael
events.summary: The LORD does as he said, and Sarah bears Isaac when Abraham is one hundred. Sarah says God has made her laugh. At Isaac’s weaning feast, Sarah sees Hagar’s son mocking. She tells Abraham to send Hagar and the boy away. Abraham is grieved, but God says to listen and promises a nation from the boy. In the wilderness the water runs out, and Hagar weeps. God hears the boy, and Hagar sees a well. Abraham and Abimelech then swear an oath over a well at Beersheba.
events.detail: Hagar leaves with bread and one container of water (verse 14). When it is empty she sits apart so she will not watch her son die. Verse 17 says twice that God heard the boy. The help in verse 19 is small and exact: she sees a well. The text does not say a well was made. It says her eyes were opened. Verse 20 adds what lasts: God was with the boy as he grew.

events.title: The binding of Isaac
events.summary: God tests Abraham and tells him to offer his son Isaac in Moriah. Abraham rises early and travels three days with Isaac and two servants. Isaac carries the wood and asks where the lamb is. Abraham says God will provide the lamb. He builds the altar, binds Isaac, and takes the knife. The LORD’s angel stops him and says he now knows Abraham fears God. Abraham offers a ram caught in a thicket. The LORD swears to bless him and all nations through his offspring.

Abraham’s answer in verse 8 is all he has: “God will provide.” The line “they both went together” comes before and after it (verses 6 and 8). Verse 13 gives the ram, and verse 14 names the place for that answer. The promise in verses 16–18 repeats 12:3 with an oath added.

events.title: Sarah's burial
events.summary: Sarah dies at Hebron at age 127, and Abraham mourns her. He tells the Hittites he is a foreigner and asks for a burial place. They offer him the best of their tombs. Abraham asks to buy the cave of Machpelah from Ephron at full price. Ephron offers the field as a gift, then names its worth: four hundred shekels. Abraham weighs out the silver before the people at the city gate. The field, cave, and trees are deeded to him. He buries Sarah there.
events.detail: God promised Abraham this land in 12:7 and 13:15. Yet in verse 4 he owns none of it and calls himself a foreigner. He is offered a free tomb twice and refuses both times. He wants a purchase made before witnesses (verses 13 and 16). Verses 17–18 read like a deed: field, cave, trees, borders, and witnesses. A grave is the first piece of the promised land he owns. A cuneiform tablet shows how another people recorded a field sale.

lds.text: Abraham secures a burial place for Sarah. He calls himself “a stranger and a foreigner” (verse 4). Why does he insist on paying in verse 13?

events.title: Rebekah meets Isaac
events.summary: Old Abraham makes his servant swear to find Isaac a wife among his relatives. The servant takes ten camels to the city of Nahor. At the well he prays for a woman who also waters his camels. Rebekah comes and does just that. He gives her gold and learns she is Bethuel’s daughter, of Abraham’s family. He tells her brother Laban the whole story, and the family agrees. They ask Rebekah, and she says, “I will go.” Isaac meets her, marries her, and loves her.
events.detail: The marriage is arranged by others for most of the chapter. Abraham sends, the servant prays, and Laban and Bethuel agree (verse 51). Yet verse 8 made the woman’s willingness a condition from the start. In verse 57 the family says, “We will call the young lady, and ask her.” Her answer in verse 58 is three words: “I will go.” Like Abram in 12:1, she leaves her family for a land unseen. Verse 60 gives her a blessing close to Abraham’s in 22:17.

lds.text: Rebekah agrees to the journey. Her family asks if she will go with the servant (verse 58). What had Abraham said about an unwilling woman in verse 8?

events.title: Abraham's death and the twins
events.summary: Abraham marries Keturah and has more sons, but he gives all he has to Isaac. He dies at 175, and Isaac and Ishmael bury him beside Sarah. Ishmael’s twelve sons are listed. Isaac prays for Rebekah, who has no child, and she conceives twins. The LORD tells her the elder will serve the younger. Esau is born first, red and hairy, and Jacob follows holding his heel. Jacob does not offer food first. He asks for a sale and then an oath (verses 31 and 33). Verse 34 lists Esau’s acts quickly: he ate, drank, rose, and left. The writer then gives a verdict: Esau “despised his birthright.”

events.title: Isaac's wells
events.summary: In a famine the LORD tells Isaac to stay and not go to Egypt. He repeats to Isaac the oath he swore to Abraham. In Gerar Isaac says Rebekah is his sister, and Abimelech finds out and rebukes him. Isaac’s crops yield a hundredfold, and the Philistines envy him. They fill his father’s wells with earth and send him away. Isaac’s men dig wells, and the herdsmen of Gerar claim two of them. He moves again, digs a third, and names it Rehoboth for the room they found. Abimelech then comes to make a peace oath at Beersheba.

The third well brings no dispute, and he credits the LORD with making room. Verse 16 says he was the stronger party, so he was not forced by weakness. Verse 28 shows the result: his rivals come to him asking for peace. They say they saw that the LORD was with him.

events.title: Jacob receives the blessing
events.summary: Isaac is old and blind and sends Esau to hunt game before he blesses him. Rebekah hears and tells Jacob to bring two goats. She dresses Jacob in Esau’s clothes and covers his hands with goat skins. Jacob tells his father he is Esau. Isaac doubts the voice, feels the hands, and blesses him as lord over his brothers. Esau returns, and Isaac trembles. Esau weeps and begs for a blessing, and plans to kill Jacob. Rebekah tells Jacob to flee to her brother Laban in Haran.

In verse 33 he says of Jacob, “Yes, he will be blessed.” Verse 37 lists what was given: rule, servants, grain, and wine. The spoken words are treated as done and cannot be shared out again. So Esau’s loss is real, and the text records his bitter cry (verse 34). Jacob gains the blessing and loses his home in the same chapter. Verse 45 shows Rebekah’s fear: losing both sons in one day.

events.title: Jacob's dream at Bethel
events.summary: Isaac blesses Jacob and sends him to Paddan Aram to marry a daughter of Laban. Esau sees this and marries a daughter of Ishmael. On the way Jacob sleeps with a stone under his head. He dreams of a stairway to heaven with angels going up and down. The LORD promises him the land, many offspring, and his presence everywhere. Jacob wakes and says the LORD is in this place. He sets up the stone, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel. He vows a tenth to God if God brings him home in peace.
events.detail: Jacob is running from Esau and has only a stone for a pillow (verse 11). God speaks first. He says, “I am with you, and will keep you, wherever you go.” Jacob’s words in verse 16 show surprise. He had not known God was there. He names the spot Bethel and calls it “God’s house” (verses 17–19). His vow in verses 20–22 still begins with “If.”

events.title: Leah and Rachel
events.summary: Jacob reaches a well near Haran and meets Rachel, Laban’s daughter. He rolls the stone away, waters her sheep, and weeps. Laban welcomes him as family. Jacob loves Rachel and works seven years for her. At the wedding feast Laban brings him Leah in the evening. Jacob protests, and Laban says the younger is not given before the firstborn. Jacob marries Rachel a week later and works seven more years. The LORD sees that Leah is unloved, and she bears Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah.

Here Laban puts the firstborn in the place of the younger. His answer in verse 26 names that very rule. Jacob, who tricked a blind father, is tricked at night. The cost falls on Leah as well, whom verse 31 calls “hated.”

lds.text: God sees Leah’s pain. Jacob asks Laban why he deceived him (verse 25). Whom had Jacob deceived in chapter 27?

events.title: Jacob's growing household
events.summary: Rachel has no children and envies Leah. She gives her servant Bilhah to Jacob, and Bilhah bears Dan and Naphtali. Leah gives her servant Zilpah, who bears Gad and Asher. Rachel trades a night with Jacob for Leah’s mandrake plants. Leah bears Issachar, Zebulun, and a daughter, Dinah. God remembers Rachel, and she bears Joseph. Jacob asks to go home, and Laban asks him to stay for wages. Jacob takes the spotted and dark animals as pay, and his flocks grow large.

Leah then tells Jacob, “I have surely hired you” (verse 16). Talk of hire and wages runs from sons to sheep (verses 18, 28, 32). People in this house are paid for and traded. Yet verses 17 and 22 say God listened to each woman in turn.

lds.text: The children’s names reveal hope and distress. Leah says Rachel has “taken away my husband” (verse 15). What do the two sisters trade?

events.title: Jacob leaves Laban
events.summary: Laban’s sons say Jacob took their father’s wealth, and Laban’s face turns cold. The LORD tells Jacob to return home. Jacob tells Rachel and Leah that Laban changed his wages ten times. They agree to go, saying their father sold them. Jacob leaves in secret, and Rachel steals her father’s household idols. Laban chases them, but God warns him in a dream. He searches the tents and finds nothing, and Jacob lists twenty years of hard service. The two men pile stones as a border and swear to do no harm.
events.detail: Jacob asks his wives before he leaves, and verses 14–16 give their answer. They speak together, though they were rivals in chapter 30. They say their father treats them as foreigners. He “sold” them and used up the money. Jacob worked fourteen years for them (verse 41). So they count the flocks God gave Jacob as rightly theirs and their children’s. Their consent turns Jacob’s flight into a family decision.

lds.text: Jacob and Laban set a boundary. Rachel and Leah say their father “has sold us” (verse 15). What do they tell Jacob to do in verse 16?

events.title: Jacob wrestles
events.summary: Angels meet Jacob on his way. He sends word to Esau, and hears that Esau is coming with four hundred men. Jacob is afraid and splits his camp in two. He prays, saying he is not worthy, and asks God to save him from Esau. He sends herds ahead as a gift, with space between them. That night he sends his family across the Jabbok and is left alone. A man wrestles with him until dawn and strains his hip. The man names him Israel, and Jacob limps away from Peniel.
events.detail: Jacob plans first: two camps, so one may escape (verses 7–8). Then he prays. Verse 11 is plain about the fear and names who could die: mothers and children. He bases the request on God’s own words (verses 9 and 12). He claims nothing for himself and says he is “not worthy” (verse 10). After the prayer he still sends gifts. He says it would wrong his master and be a sin against God. One day she grabs his garment, and he runs out and leaves it. She tells the household and her husband that the Hebrew servant came at her. events.title: Joseph before Pharaoh
events.summary: Two years later Pharaoh dreams of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones. He also dreams of seven good heads of grain swallowed by seven thin ones. No wise man can explain it, and the cup bearer remembers Joseph. Joseph says the answer is not in him but comes from God. The dreams mean seven years of plenty and then seven of famine. He advises storing a fifth of each harvest under a wise man. Pharaoh sets Joseph over all Egypt and gives him his ring and a wife. Joseph stores grain, has two sons, and sells grain when the famine comes.

Verse 36 states its purpose: “that the land will not perish.” The stored grain is held “under the hand of Pharaoh” (verse 35). So saving lives and growing the king’s power arrive together. events.title: Benjamin goes to Egypt
events.summary: The grain runs out, and Jacob tells his sons to buy more. Judah says they cannot go without Benjamin. He offers himself as a pledge for the boy’s return. Israel agrees and sends gifts and double money. In Egypt, Joseph has the brothers brought to his house, and they fear a trap. The steward calms them and brings Simeon out. Joseph sees Benjamin, leaves the room, and weeps. The brothers are seated by age, and Benjamin gets five times as much food.

events.title: Joseph reveals himself

events.title: Jacob goes to Egypt

Jacob’s sons carry him, their wives, and their children in Pharaoh’s wagons. The chapter lists the family by mother, seventy people in all. Judah goes ahead to lead the way to Goshen. events.title: Jacob's final words

Zebulun, Issachar, Dan, Gad, Asher, and Naphtali each get a short saying. Joseph is a fruitful vine, helped by the Mighty One of Jacob. Benjamin is a hungry wolf. ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time. Exodus 13:17 names a near road, “the way of the land of the Philistines.” The encyclopedia article lists that name for this coast road.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time. Numbers 20:17 and 21:22 name “the king’s highway” east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

guides.title: Genesis: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Creation gives people a shared worth
steps.text: Six times the chapter says God saw that his work was good. People come last, and verse 31 says “very good.” Verse 27 says “image” twice and then names both male and female. No one group holds that standing alone. The command to rule in verse 28 comes after the blessing. Verses 29–30 then give plants as food to people and animals alike. So ruling here sits beside care for life that God called good.

steps.title: A grave becomes a claim to land
steps.text: God promised Abraham this land in 12:7 and 13:15. Yet in verse 4 he owns none of it and calls himself a foreigner. He is offered a free tomb twice and refuses both times. He wants a purchase made before witnesses (verses 13 and 16). Verses 17–18 read like a deed: field, cave, trees, borders, and witnesses. A grave is the first piece of the promised land he owns. A cuneiform tablet shows how another people recorded a field sale.

steps.title: Food storage creates political power
steps.text: Pharaoh asked for a meaning, and Joseph adds a plan (verses 33–36). The plan is practical: overseers, a fifth of each harvest, and stores in the cities. Verse 36 states its purpose: “that the land will not perish.” The stored grain is held “under the hand of Pharaoh” (verse 35). So saving lives and growing the king’s power arrive together. Chapter 47 shows what that power later costs the people. An Egyptian granary model shows scribes recording grain, as a comparison only.

chapterMaps.narrative: In the beginning God creates the heavens and the earth. He speaks, and light, sky, land, and plants appear over three days. Sun, moon, stars, sea animals, and birds follow. On the sixth day he makes land animals and then people. He makes people in his own image, male and female. He blesses them and tells them to fill the earth and rule the animals. He gives plants as food to people and animals. God sees all he has made and calls it very good.

God plants a garden in Eden with a river and two named trees. He puts the man there to work it and keep it. He forbids one tree and warns of death. God says it is not good for the man to be alone. The man names the animals, but none is a helper like him. God makes a woman from his rib, and the man welcomes her as his flesh.

She sees the fruit is good, eats, and gives some to her husband. Their eyes open, and they cover themselves and hide. God asks where the man is and whether he ate. The man blames the woman, and the woman blames the serpent. God curses the serpent and the ground, and speaks of pain and hard work. He clothes them with skins and sends them out of Eden.

Cain’s family builds a city, and Lamech boasts of killing a man. Eve bears Seth, and people begin to call on the LORD’s name.

He decides to wipe out people and animals. But Noah finds favor and walks with God. God tells Noah the earth is filled with violence. He orders a ship of gopher wood with three levels and one door. Noah is to bring his family, pairs of animals, and food, and he obeys.

After seven days the deep bursts open and the sky’s windows open. Rain falls forty days and nights. Noah’s family and the animals go in, and the LORD shuts him in. The dove comes back with an olive leaf, then does not return. God tells Noah to leave the ship with his family and the animals. Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings. God will demand a reckoning for human life, because he made people in his image. He makes a covenant with Noah, his family, and every living creature. No flood will destroy the earth again, and the rainbow is the sign. Noah plants a vineyard and gets drunk. Ham sees his father naked, and Shem and Japheth cover him. textRoutes.title: Babel and Terah's family
textRoutes.summary: All people speak one language and settle on a plain in Shinar. They bake bricks and plan a city with a tower to the sky. They want a name for themselves and fear being scattered. The LORD comes down to see, confuses their language, and scatters them. The city is called Babel. Then the record runs from Shem to Terah. Terah fathers Abram, Nahor, and Haran, and Abram’s wife Sarai has no child. Terah leaves Ur for Canaan but settles in Haran and dies there.
textRoutes.detail: Verse 4 gives the builders two aims. They want a name, and they want not to be scattered. God had told people to fill the earth in 1:28 and 9:1. The tower should reach the sky, yet the LORD “came down” to see it. They get the very thing they feared: scattering (verse 8). In 12:2 God offers Abram a great name as a gift. The chapter sets a name people grab beside a name God gives.

textRoutes.title: Abram's call
textRoutes.summary: The LORD tells Abram to leave his country and his father’s house. He promises a great nation and a blessing for all families through Abram. Abram goes at age seventy-five with Sarai and Lot. In Canaan the LORD promises the land to his offspring, and Abram builds altars. A famine sends him to Egypt. He asks Sarai to say she is his sister, because he fears being killed. Pharaoh takes her and pays Abram well, and the LORD sends plagues. Pharaoh rebukes Abram and sends them away.
textRoutes.detail: The promise in verses 2–3 has seven parts and ends outside Abram’s family. All the families of the earth are to be blessed through him. The rest of the chapter tests that at once. In Egypt Abram protects himself with a false story (verse 13). Pharaoh’s house gets plagues, not blessing (verse 17). A foreign king then corrects the man God chose (verses 18–19). The promise stands, but the chapter shows it does not depend on Abram’s good conduct.

textRoutes.title: Abram and Lot separate
textRoutes.summary: Abram returns from Egypt to Bethel, rich in livestock, silver, and gold. Lot also has flocks, and the land cannot hold both. Their herdsmen quarrel. Abram asks for no strife and offers Lot his choice of land. Lot sees the well-watered Jordan plain and chooses it. He camps near Sodom, whose men are very wicked. The LORD tells Abram to look all around, for the land will be his. Abram moves to the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and builds an altar.
textRoutes.detail: Abram is the uncle, and the land was promised to him (12:7). He could choose first. Verse 9 gives the choice to Lot. His stated reason in verse 8 is “we are relatives.” Verse 10 shows Lot choosing by what his eyes see. Verse 13 warns what was near that green plain. After Lot leaves, the LORD tells Abram to look, and gives him all.

textRoutes.title: Lot rescued
textRoutes.summary: Four kings make war on five kings near the Salt Sea. The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah flee, and the winners take goods, food, and people. They take Lot, who lives in Sodom. Abram leads 318 trained men, attacks by night, and brings everyone back. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine. He blesses Abram, and Abram gives him a tenth. The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods. Abram refuses even a thread, so the king cannot say he made Abram rich.
textRoutes.detail: Two kings meet Abram after the battle. Melchizedek blesses him and credits God with the win (verse 20). Abram gives him a tenth. The king of Sodom offers goods, and Abram takes nothing. Verse 23 gives his reason: no king may say, “I have made Abram rich.” A gift from a ruler could become a claim on him. Verse 24 keeps his rule from costing his allies their share.

textRoutes.title: Sodom and Lot's escape
textRoutes.summary: Two angels come to Sodom, and Lot urges them to stay in his house. The men of the city surround it and demand the guests. Lot offers his two daughters, and the crowd turns on him. The angels pull Lot in and strike the men blind. They warn that the LORD will destroy the city, but Lot’s sons-in-law think he jokes. At dawn the angels drag Lot, his wife, and his daughters out. Fire and sulfur fall, and Lot’s wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. In a cave, Lot’s daughters make him drunk and bear Moab and Ben Ammi.
textRoutes.detail: Lot takes the guests in and tries to protect them. His way of doing it is to offer his daughters (verse 8). The text reports this without praise. His reason is that the men are “under the shadow of my roof.” He guards guests and gives up the people who most depend on him. The angels, not Lot, save everyone in the house (verses 10–11). Verse 29 says Lot was spared because God remembered Abraham.

textRoutes.title: The binding of Isaac
textRoutes.summary: God tests Abraham and tells him to offer his son Isaac in Moriah. Abraham rises early and travels three days with Isaac and two servants. Isaac carries the wood and asks where the lamb is. Abraham says God will provide the lamb. He builds the altar, binds Isaac, and takes the knife. The LORD’s angel stops him and says he now knows Abraham fears God. Abraham offers a ram caught in a thicket. The LORD swears to bless him and all nations through his offspring.
textRoutes.detail: Verse 1 tells the reader this is a test. Abraham and Isaac are not told. So Isaac’s question in verse 7 is asked in the dark. Abraham’s answer in verse 8 is all he has: “God will provide.” The line “they both went together” comes before and after it (verses 6 and 8). Verse 13 gives the ram, and verse 14 names the place for that answer. The promise in verses 16–18 repeats 12:3 with an oath added.

textRoutes.title: Rebekah meets Isaac
textRoutes.summary: Old Abraham makes his servant swear to find Isaac a wife among his relatives. The servant takes ten camels to the city of Nahor. At the well he prays for a woman who also waters his camels. Rebekah comes and does just that. He gives her gold and learns she is Bethuel’s daughter, of Abraham’s family. He tells her brother Laban the whole story, and the family agrees. They ask Rebekah, and she says, “I will go.” Isaac meets her, marries her, and loves her.
textRoutes.detail: The marriage is arranged by others for most of the chapter. Abraham sends, the servant prays, and Laban and Bethuel agree (verse 51). Yet verse 8 made the woman’s willingness a condition from the start. In verse 57 the family says, “We will call the young lady, and ask her.” Her answer in verse 58 is three words: “I will go.” Like Abram in 12:1, she leaves her family for a land unseen. Verse 60 gives her a blessing close to Abraham’s in 22:17.

textRoutes.title: Jacob's dream at Bethel
textRoutes.summary: Isaac blesses Jacob and sends him to Paddan Aram to marry a daughter of Laban. Esau sees this and marries a daughter of Ishmael. On the way Jacob sleeps with a stone under his head. He dreams of a stairway to heaven with angels going up and down. The LORD promises him the land, many offspring, and his presence everywhere. Jacob wakes and says the LORD is in this place. He sets up the stone, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel. He vows a tenth to God if God brings him home in peace.
textRoutes.detail: Jacob is running from Esau and has only a stone for a pillow (verse 11). God speaks first. He says, “I am with you, and will keep you, wherever you go.” Jacob’s words in verse 16 show surprise. He had not known God was there. He names the spot Bethel and calls it “God’s house” (verses 17–19). His vow in verses 20–22 still begins with “If.”

textRoutes.title: Jacob leaves Laban
textRoutes.summary: Laban’s sons say Jacob took their father’s wealth, and Laban’s face turns cold. The LORD tells Jacob to return home. Jacob tells Rachel and Leah that Laban changed his wages ten times. They agree to go, saying their father sold them. Jacob leaves in secret, and Rachel steals her father’s household idols. Laban chases them, but God warns him in a dream. He searches the tents and finds nothing, and Jacob lists twenty years of hard service. The two men pile stones as a border and swear to do no harm.
textRoutes.detail: Jacob asks his wives before he leaves, and verses 14–16 give their answer. They speak together, though they were rivals in chapter 30. They say their father treats them as foreigners. He “sold” them and used up the money. Jacob worked fourteen years for them (verse 41). So they count the flocks God gave Jacob as rightly theirs and their children’s. Their consent turns Jacob’s flight into a family decision.

textRoutes.title: Jacob and Esau meet
textRoutes.summary: Jacob sees Esau coming with four hundred men. He lines up the women and children and goes ahead, bowing seven times. Esau runs to him, hugs him, and they weep. Esau asks about the family and about the herds he met. Esau says he has enough, but Jacob urges him to take the gift. Esau offers to travel together, but Jacob says his children and flocks are slow. Esau returns to Seir. Jacob goes to Succoth and then Shechem, buys land, and builds an altar.
textRoutes.detail: Jacob expected an attack and arranged his family for one (verses 1–2). Verse 4 gives five quick acts: ran, embraced, fell on his neck, kissed, wept. Jacob had just named a place Peniel for seeing God’s face and living (32:30). In verse 10 he says the same of Esau’s face. He expected judgment from both and was spared by both. He urges Esau to accept the gift, and Esau does (verse 11).

textRoutes.title: Return to Bethel
textRoutes.summary: God tells Jacob to go up to Bethel and build an altar. Jacob tells his household to put away foreign gods and make themselves clean. They hand over the gods and earrings, and he buries them under an oak. At Bethel God blesses him, repeats the name Israel, and promises the land. Rebekah’s nurse Deborah dies there. On the road Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin and is buried near Bethlehem. Reuben lies with Bilhah, his father’s concubine. Jacob reaches Isaac at Hebron, and Esau and Jacob bury their father.
textRoutes.detail: God’s order in verse 1 is to Jacob alone: go, live there, build an altar. Jacob turns it into orders for everyone with him (verse 2). The first is to give up foreign gods. Rachel had taken her father’s idols in 31:19. So the journey to Bethel begins by clearing the camp. Verse 3 gives Jacob’s reason: God answered him in distress and stayed with him. That is the promise of 28:15, now reported as kept.

textRoutes.title: Joseph sold
textRoutes.summary: Israel loves seventeen-year-old Joseph most and gives him a tunic of many colors. His brothers hate him more when he dreams that they bow to him. Jacob sends Joseph to check on his brothers near Shechem. They plan to kill him, but Reuben persuades them to throw him in a pit. Judah proposes selling him, and he is sold for twenty pieces of silver. The brothers dip his tunic in goat’s blood and show it to their father. Jacob decides an animal killed Joseph and refuses comfort. In Egypt Joseph is sold to Potiphar, Pharaoh’s captain of the guard.
textRoutes.detail: The brothers never say Joseph is dead. In verse 32 they hand over the tunic and ask their father to examine it. Jacob supplies the false story himself in verse 33. The tunic was the sign of his favor in verse 3. Now it is the proof of his loss. Jacob once deceived his father with goat skins and a brother’s clothes (27:15–16). Here a goat’s blood and a son’s clothes deceive him.

textRoutes.title: Benjamin goes to Egypt
textRoutes.summary: The grain runs out, and Jacob tells his sons to buy more. Judah says they cannot go without Benjamin. He offers himself as a pledge for the boy’s return. Israel agrees and sends gifts and double money. In Egypt, Joseph has the brothers brought to his house, and they fear a trap. The steward calms them and brings Simeon out. Joseph sees Benjamin, leaves the room, and weeps. The brothers are seated by age, and Benjamin gets five times as much food.
textRoutes.detail: Reuben offered his two sons’ lives as a pledge in 42:37, and Jacob refused. Judah offers himself in verse 9. He does not promise that nothing will go wrong. He promises to carry the blame “forever” if it does. In 37:26–27 Judah was the one who proposed selling Joseph. Verse 8 gives his reason now: so that the whole family may live. Jacob accepts in verses 11–14 and lets Benjamin go.

textRoutes.title: Jacob goes to Egypt
textRoutes.summary: Israel sets out and offers sacrifices at Beersheba. God tells him in a night vision not to fear going to Egypt. God will make him a great nation there and bring him back. Jacob’s sons carry him, their wives, and their children in Pharaoh’s wagons. The chapter lists the family by mother, seventy people in all. Judah goes ahead to lead the way to Goshen. Joseph meets his father and weeps on his neck for a long time. He tells his brothers to say they are herdsmen, so they can live in Goshen.
textRoutes.detail: Joseph coaches his brothers on one answer for Pharaoh: they keep livestock. Verse 34 gives the reason. Egyptians look down on shepherds, so the family will be settled apart in Goshen. The low standing of their trade becomes their protection. Living apart, they can stay one family. God’s promise in verse 3 is that they will become a nation there. Verse 4 adds that he will bring them up again.

textRoutes.title: Burial and forgiveness
textRoutes.summary: Joseph weeps over his father and has him embalmed. Egypt mourns seventy days. With Pharaoh’s leave, Joseph and a great company bury Jacob in the cave at Machpelah. Back in Egypt the brothers fear that Joseph will now repay them. They send a message asking forgiveness and bow before him. Joseph weeps and tells them not to fear. He says they meant evil, but God meant it for good, to save many lives. Dying at 110, he makes Israel swear to carry his bones out of Egypt.
textRoutes.detail: Seventeen years have passed since Joseph forgave his brothers (45:5; 47:28). Verse 15 shows they still fear him once their father is gone. They offer to be his slaves in verse 18. Joseph answers with a question: “Am I in the place of God?” He will not take the judge’s seat. Verse 20 keeps both truths from chapter 45: they meant evil, and God meant good. Verse 21 turns forgiveness into a promise to feed them and their children.
